title: Choose the visual world for DSSantos Terminal
question: The roll assigned the Signal Box Panel. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: Signal Box Panel
options.lineage: Railway control panels: UK NX panels, Swiss Domino tile panels, Japanese CTC boards
options.thesis: The profile is a working signalling panel. Your stack is the track layout, your work is the trains moving through it, and the interlocking logic is code.
options.viewport: A wide panel mimic: the name plate engraved above a track diagram where five coloured routes (backend, database, frontend, data, tools) meet at an interchange called TERMINAL. A headcode train lights its way across track sections, one at a time.
options.risk: Signalling is niche: non-transit visitors need clear labels to read the diagram and not just admire it.

raised.raise: Data density: describer berths and timings set as tight tabular mono numerals that carry real facts, with no decorative filler.
No glow and no gradient: depth comes only from flat stacked tiles and plates, and lit states are flat fills.
One engraving face carries the name plate and the smallest label alike.
One reserved colour: signal red means only 'occupied / not yet open' (Ferret, Unity), never decoration.

options.label: LED Passenger Display
options.lineage: On-board and platform dot-matrix passenger information displays
options.thesis: The bus 'next stop' display you build at work, turned into the profile. Every letter is literally made of dots and bits.
options.viewport: A wide amber dot-matrix display reads 'DANIEL SANTOS ▸ FULLSTACK · TRANSIT', and a ticker scrolls through the stack as upcoming stops.
options.risk: Familiar: dot-matrix and terminal looks are where most 'transit dev' profiles land.

options.label: Teletext Travel Pages
options.thesis: The profile as a teletext service: P100 index, a P4xx travel magazine, every section a numbered page.
options.viewport: P100 header with page counter, double-height name in yellow, and a mosaic tram drawn from blocks.
options.case: Fuses cleanly, and the text grid is very legible. It loses on audience identification: teletext speaks to retro nerds more than to transit or code.
options.risk: Reads as retro novelty when the grid is not strict.

options.label: Azulejo Station Hall
options.thesis: The profile as cobalt tile panels narrating a career in the grammar of a Portuguese station hall.
options.viewport: A cobalt tile panel of a tram and train across the grid seams, with a cartouche naming DSSANTOS TERMINAL.
options.case: Strong cultural home for a Portuguese transit dev. It loses on product clarity: code barely appears, and you chose a global mashup over one city.

options.label: Datamatics Field
options.thesis: Transit data as pure black-and-white barcode fields.
options.case: Loses both axes: no transit identification, and the facts get buried.
options.kept: Data density: real numbers, tight tabular mono.

options.label: Layered Papercut
options.thesis: A symmetrical roundel of layered paper.
options.risk: No relation to transit or code.
options.kept: Depth by overlap only: no gradients, no glow.

options.label: Design Annual Plates
options.risk: Too quiet: the 'stale' you want to leave behind.

options.label: Couture Doll Atelier
options.thesis: Each project as a numbered look.
options.kept: One reserved colour for one meaning.

canonCard.label: The GitHub profile standard
canonCard.thesis: Typing-SVG header, shields.io badge rows, github-readme-stats cards, played straight and clean.
canonCard.viewport: Centered typing header, an about paragraph, badge grid, two stats cards side by side.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from thousands of profiles by design.
